_comment: Bian's words for the English edition of Part 4, 'Is Oil Palm Really Burning
Kalimantan?', one entry per segment of jadwalPulauEN.json's urutan, the same
scene ids as the Indonesian. tts_konsesi.py --film pulau --bahasa en generates
each clip from here; the mp3s are gitignored.
A translation of src/narasiPulau.json; every figure and caveat is the same
(see its _comment for where each comes from). No company is named.

teks.01-kilas: Is oil palm really burning Kalimantan? In the three earlier parts, four concessions on the Ketapang coast burned worse than the land around them. This time we test it across the whole island.
teks.02-banding: We compared more than a thousand concessions, oil palm and pulpwood plantations, with similar land that has no permit: the same peat depth, the same land cover, the same fire history, the same distance to rivers and settlements, and the same severity of drought. In all, thirteen million cells, each two hundred metres across.
teks.03-pulau: The answer is surprising. At the same drought, concessions across Kalimantan did not burn more than similar land without a permit, whether oil palm or pulpwood. If drought is not matched, oil palm even seems to burn less. Part of that gap appears because many oil palm concessions lie where the dry season was milder.
teks.04-sedikit: But the average hides an imbalance. Of nine hundred and eight oil palm concessions, fifty-one burned far more than similar land. Only six percent, yet they account for two fifths of all the burned area in oil palm concessions. Among pulpwood plantations, fourteen concessions account for about half. All four Ketapang concessions are among them.
teks.05-gambut: What sets them apart? For oil palm, not the company group, not the permit status, and not an R-S-P-O certificate. Peat raises the odds. The more peat inside a concession, and the deeper it is, the more likely the concession is to burn in excess, on two peat maps made independently. But peat is not the whole answer. Almost six in ten of the oil palm concessions that burned in excess have no peat.
teks.06-bersih: Was fire used to clear land? If it was, burned land would soon be planted. Of the land that burned in twenty fifteen, only two point four percent became oil palm within six years, almost the same as land that did not burn. And almost no land was cleared before the fire came. In oil palm concessions, we found no evidence of fire being used to clear land. In pulpwood plantations, burned land was planted more often, though from a small base.
teks.07-kering: What about timing? Without matching drought, oil palm land seems to start burning earlier, while the drought is still milder. But once drought is matched, the gap shrinks, and it can no longer be told apart from zero. We cannot say that concessions ignite earlier.
teks.08-batas: So why did Kalimantan burn so badly, while Sabah and Sarawak barely did? Mostly because of rain. The drought came from the south. Southern Kalimantan received only a seventh of its normal rain, while the north of the island, including Malaysia, stayed wet. But where the weather was the same, land on the Indonesian side still burned about four times as much.
teks.09-tutup: So, is oil palm really burning Kalimantan? Not in general. At the same drought, concessions did not burn more than similar land. The problem lies with a small group of concessions that burned far more. Peat raises the odds, but most of those concessions have no peat, and the cause has not been measured. The public concession boundaries date from twenty twelve, and these results have not yet been peer reviewed.
